title: Building the contract of employment
subtitle: Express terms, implied terms and the statutory statement
objectives: Distinguish express terms from terms implied in fact (business efficacy, custom and practice) and terms implied by law or statute
State the effect of the s 1 ERA 1996 written statement of particulars, and explain why it is evidence of the contract's terms rather than the contract itself
Explain how a collective agreement can become incorporated into an individual contract of employment, and identify the limits of that incorporation

leadingAuthorities.role: Requires a written statement of the main particulars of employment, given no later than the first day of work
Revisited here on terms: courts may look past written wording to identify the terms actually agreed

leadingAuthorities.citation: National Coal Board v Galley [1958] 1 WLR 16
leadingAuthorities.role: A collective agreement's terms can be incorporated into, and bind, the individual contract of employment

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Once status is settled, the next question in almost any employment dispute is: what did the parties actually agree to? Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can name the categories of term — this lesson checks whether you can find each one inside a messy fact pattern.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans towards scenario questions: expect a fact pattern where you have to identify which category a term falls into, not a definition to restate.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — the distinction between express, implied and statutory-derived terms is the scaffolding the rest of this lesson assumes you already have.

overview.hook: Ask most new employees what's in their contract and they'll describe the document HR emailed them: pay, hours, job title, holiday entitlement. That document is important — but it is not the whole contract, and in a surprising number of disputes it isn't even conclusive evidence of the contract. Custom, practice, unwritten expectations and even a document neither side signed can all end up binding both parties just as firmly as anything typed up and handed over on day one.

parts.heading: Four places a term can come from
parts.voice: structural — a map students will return to as a reference
body: A contract of employment is built from more sources than most other contracts, and exam questions in this area are usually really asking: which source does this term come from, and how much weight does it carry?

Express terms are those actually agreed, whether in writing, orally, or partly both — and they take priority where they genuinely reflect what was agreed. Terms implied in fact fill gaps the parties didn't address, using tests like business efficacy (the term is necessary to make the contract work at all) or custom and practice (a practice so well established in the workplace or industry that both sides are taken to have contracted on that basis). Terms implied by law apply to employment contracts generally, by virtue of being employment contracts, regardless of what these particular parties intended — the duty of mutual trust and confidence is the best-known example. And terms can be incorporated from an external source, most commonly a collective agreement negotiated between an employer and a trade union.

None of these sources is self-executing: a term is only part of the contract if it satisfies the relevant test for how it gets there. A great deal of first-year confusion in this topic comes from treating 'it's written down somewhere' as sufficient on its own.

components.label: Four sources of contractual terms
points: Express terms — actually agreed, in writing or orally, or a mix of both
Terms implied in fact — business efficacy (necessary to make the contract work) or custom and practice (well established, certain, reasonable and notorious)
Terms implied by law — apply to all employment contracts as a class, e.g. mutual trust and confidence
Incorporated terms — drawn from an external source, most commonly a collective agreement, and made part of the individual contract by an express or implied incorporation clause

interaction.prompt: Is the duty of mutual trust and confidence typically an express term or a term implied by law?
options: A term implied by law, applying to employment contracts as a class
An express term, only present where the written contract specifically states it
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Mutual trust and confidence is the textbook example of a term implied by law — it exists because the contract is an employment contract, not because either party wrote it in.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — this duty is implied by law into employment contracts generally. It doesn't need to be, and usually isn't, spelled out in the written agreement to apply.

parts.heading: Section 1 ERA 1996: a statement, not the contract
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: Every worker is entitled, from the first day of employment, to a written statement setting out the main particulars of their engagement — pay, hours, holiday entitlement, notice periods, job title, and more, following the wider disclosure requirements introduced by the 'Good Work Plan' reforms in force since 6 April 2020.

The most tested point in this whole area is what the s 1 statement legally is. It is **not** the contract of employment, and it is not, by itself, conclusive proof of what the terms actually are — it is a statutory document the employer is obliged to produce, and it is evidence of the contract, carrying real but rebuttable weight. Where the written statement conflicts with what the parties actually agreed, or with the reality of how the relationship operates, the statement can be shown to be wrong — the same reality-over-paperwork principle from Autoclenz applies here just as it does to a full written contract.

This matters practically: a worker who never received a s 1 statement at all is not thereby left without a contract — the contract exists from the moment work begins on agreed terms, express or implied, and the s 1 statement is simply a (compulsory) record of it, not its source.

components.text: Where an employee begins employment with an employer, the employer shall give to the employee a written statement of particulars of employment. The statement may (subject to section 2(4)) be given in instalments and (whether or not given in instalments) shall be given not later than the beginning of the employment.
elements: Applies from the first day of employment (a 'day one' right since 6 April 2020)
Covers the main particulars: pay, hours, holiday, notice, job title, place of work, and other prescribed items
Is evidence of the contract's terms, not the contract itself, and can be shown to be inaccurate

interaction.prompt: By when must an employer provide the s 1 ERA 1996 written statement of particulars?
options: Not later than the beginning of the employment
Within two months of the employment starting
Only if the employee requests it in writing
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Since the 2020 reforms this is a day-one right — the statement must be given no later than the start of employment, not within a grace period afterwards.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at the timing. This is now a day-one right: the statement must be given no later than the beginning of the employment, not within any later window.

parts.heading: Filling the gaps: business efficacy and custom and practice
parts.voice: case-narrative — works through worked examples of each test
body: Terms implied in fact exist to fill genuine gaps — situations the express terms simply don't address, where the contract needs a rule to function at all, or where a settled workplace practice has become part of what both sides understood they were agreeing to.

The business efficacy test asks whether a term is necessary to make the contract work as a functioning agreement — not merely reasonable, not merely something the tribunal thinks would have been sensible to include, but something so obviously necessary that both parties must be taken to have intended it, even though they never said so. A term implied on custom and practice, by contrast, asks a different question: has this practice been followed so consistently, and is it so well known, certain and reasonable within the workplace or industry, that employees are taken to have contracted on the assumption it would continue?

The two tests can point to the same practical outcome — a term neither side wrote down nonetheless binding both — but they get there differently, and an exam answer that conflates them (arguing necessity where the real evidence is a longstanding, notorious workplace practice, or vice versa) will lose marks even if the final conclusion happens to be right.

components.definition: A workplace or industry practice implied as a contractual term where it is reasonable, certain, and so well known ('notorious') that both employer and employee are taken to have contracted on the understanding it would continue — distinct from business efficacy, which asks whether a term is necessary to make the contract function at all.

interaction.prompt: Put these questions in the order a tribunal works through when deciding whether a practice has become an implied term by custom and practice.
items: Is the practice certain — clear and consistently applied, not ad hoc?
Is the practice well known ('notorious') within the workplace or industry?
Conclude whether employees can be taken to have contracted on the basis it would continue

parts.heading: Autoclenz revisited: the same reality test applies to terms
parts.voice: argumentative — connects the case back to a different doctrinal question
body: Autoclenz Ltd v Belcher appeared in Lesson 1 as a status case, but its reasoning applies with equal force one level down, to the individual terms of a contract that everyone agrees is a contract of employment. The same inequality-of-bargaining-power reasoning that let the Supreme Court disregard a false 'self-employed' label applies just as readily to a false term buried inside an otherwise genuine employment contract — a clause stating something the parties never actually intended to be bound by, or that the actual working practice has simply overtaken.

This matters because the s 1 statement and any accompanying written contract are drafted by the employer, almost always without individual negotiation. A term that looks unambiguous on the page — 'the employee has no entitlement to overtime pay' — can be shown not to reflect the true agreement if, in practice, overtime has always been paid as a matter of course and both sides understood that to be the deal.

The lesson for exam technique: a written term is a strong starting point, not the end of the analysis. Always ask whether the facts given actually support that term being the true, operative agreement, or whether — as in Autoclenz — the paperwork and the reality have quietly diverged.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume that once a term is 'in the written contract', that settles the matter and no further analysis is needed.
components.whyItsWrong: Autoclenz shows a written term can be disregarded where the evidence — including how the parties have actually behaved — shows it doesn't reflect the true agreement. This is particularly live wherever there is unequal bargaining power, which describes most employment relationships by default.

interaction.prompt: In the extract below, highlight the sentence most directly relevant to whether a written term about pay can be displaced by practice.
interaction.passage: A written term will ordinarily be strong evidence of what was agreed. But where the evidence, including the way the parties have subsequently conducted themselves, shows that a term does not reflect what was actually agreed between them, a tribunal is entitled to find the true term rather than the one recorded on paper.
interaction.ratioSentence: Where the evidence, including the way the parties have subsequently conducted themselves, shows that a term does not reflect what was actually agreed between them, a tribunal is entitled to find the true term rather than the one recorded on paper.

parts.heading: Collective agreements: someone else's negotiation, binding your contract
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story of the leading case before drawing out the principle
body: A collective agreement is negotiated between an employer (or employers' association) and a trade union, and it is not, by itself, a legally enforceable contract between those two parties — collective agreements are presumed not to be legally binding as between employer and union unless they say otherwise. But its terms can still bind an individual employee, if they are incorporated into that employee's individual contract of employment.

National Coal Board v Galley concerned a colliery deputy whose written contract stated that his terms of employment would include those agreed from time to time between the National Coal Board and the relevant union. A later collective agreement changed working arrangements to include Saturday working; Galley refused to comply, arguing the change wasn't something he had personally agreed to. The court held that the incorporation clause in his individual contract meant the collectively agreed variation bound him automatically — he did not need to separately consent to each change, because he had already agreed, at the outset, to be bound by whatever the collective process produced.

The key point for exam purposes: incorporation requires a route in — an express clause (most common, and what Galley had) or, less often, an implied one through consistent custom and practice. Without that route in, a collective agreement remains exactly what it presumptively is: an agreement between employer and union, binding neither of them in the courts, and binding the individual employee not at all.

components.factsShort: A colliery deputy's contract incorporated terms 'agreed from time to time' between the Coal Board and his union; a later collective agreement introduced Saturday working, and he refused to comply.
components.ratioShort: Where an individual contract expressly incorporates terms agreed collectively from time to time, a later collective variation binds the employee automatically, without separate individual consent.

expanded.facts: Galley's contract of employment expressly provided that his terms would be those agreed between the National Coal Board and the relevant trade union 'from time to time'. A subsequent collective agreement altered working arrangements to require Saturday shifts as part of normal rostering. Galley declined to work the new pattern, arguing he had never personally agreed to it.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that the incorporation clause in Galley's individual contract meant he was bound by the collective agreement as varied from time to time, without any need for separate, specific consent to each change — his consent had already been given, in advance, by agreeing to the incorporation clause itself.
expanded.significance: This is the leading illustration of how a collective agreement, though not itself enforceable as between employer and union, can bind an individual employee through incorporation — and of how an incorporation clause can validly bind an employee to future changes agreed collectively, not only the terms in force when the contract was signed.

interaction.prompt: Which of these two scenarios shows a valid incorporation of a collective agreement into an individual contract?
interaction.scenarioA: Ahmed's written contract states his pay and hours will be 'as agreed from time to time between the company and the recognised trade union'; a later collectively agreed pay rise applies to him without further signature.
interaction.scenarioB: A trade union and an employer sign a collective agreement about redundancy selection criteria, but no individual employee's contract refers to collective agreements at all, and none has ever consistently applied its terms.
interaction.explanation: A has the express incorporation clause Galley requires — the individual contract itself pulls in whatever is agreed collectively. B has a collective agreement with no route into any individual contract at all, so, following the default presumption against legal enforceability between employer and union, it binds no individual employee.

testPool.prompt: Name the four sources from which a term in a contract of employment can derive.
acceptableAnswers: express terms, terms implied in fact, terms implied by law, incorporated terms
express, implied in fact, implied by law, incorporated (e.g. from a collective agreement)
testPool.modelAnswer: Express terms; terms implied in fact (business efficacy or custom and practice); terms implied by law; and terms incorporated from an external source such as a collective agreement.

testPool.prompt: By what point in the employment relationship must an employer give the s 1 ERA 1996 written statement of particulars?
acceptableAnswers: no later than the first day of employment
by the beginning of the employment
testPool.modelAnswer: No later than the beginning of the employment — this has been a day-one right since 6 April 2020.

testPool.prompt: Is the s 1 ERA 1996 written statement of particulars the same thing as the contract of employment?
options: No — it is evidence of the contract's terms, not the contract itself
Yes — the statement and the contract are legally identical documents

testPool.prompt: An employee never receives a s 1 written statement at all. What is the effect on their contract of employment?
options: They have no enforceable contract of employment until the statement is provided
Their contract still exists on whatever terms were actually agreed, express or implied — the missing statement is a separate breach of a statutory duty, not the absence of a contract
The default statutory terms in the Working Time Regulations automatically become their entire contract
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to treat the statement as constitutive of the contract, so that no statement means no contract. That's wrong: the contract arises from the parties' actual agreement (express or implied) once work begins; the statement is a compulsory record of it, and its absence is simply a separate failure by the employer.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a collective agreement between an employer and a trade union is, by default, legally enforceable as a contract between those two parties?
sliderLabels: Confident it is legally binding between them by default
Confident it is presumed not legally binding between them
testPool.correctPosition: Confident it is presumed not legally binding between them
testPool.explanation: Collective agreements are presumed not to be intended as legally enforceable contracts between employer and union unless the agreement says otherwise. Their legal force over individuals comes instead through incorporation into individual contracts of employment.

testPool.prompt: The s 1 ERA 1996 statement covers 'main particulars' of employment. Which of these is a main particular the statement must typically address?
options: The names of the employee's family members
Pay, hours and holiday entitlement
The employer's five-year business plan

testPool.prompt: Put these steps in the order a tribunal follows when an employee argues a written term does not reflect the true agreement, applying Autoclenz.
items: Identify the term as written in the document
Assess the relative bargaining power of the parties
Examine all the evidence, including subsequent conduct, of what was actually agreed and practised
Find the true term, which may differ from the written wording

testPool.prompt: Which scenario better illustrates a term implied by custom and practice, rather than business efficacy?
testPool.scenarioA: For fifteen years, every employee at a factory has received a paid extra day off around a local festival, so consistently and so well known within the workforce that new starters are told about it as a matter of course.
testPool.scenarioB: A contract says nothing about who bears the cost of a tool the employee must use, and without an implied term allocating that cost, the whole arrangement for doing the job makes no practical sense at all.
testPool.explanation: A is custom and practice: a long-standing, certain and notorious workplace practice. B is business efficacy: a term necessary to make the contract function, not a matter of established practice.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that most strongly supports an implied term by custom and practice in this scenario.
testPool.scenarioText: Maria's written contract is silent on Christmas bonuses. Every employee at her company has received a discretionary-sounding 'Christmas bonus' every single year for the last twenty years, of a broadly consistent amount, and staff routinely plan their December finances around receiving it.
tappableSpans: every single year for the last twenty years
testPool.correctSpan: every single year for the last twenty years
testPool.explanation: Consistency over a long period is the core of the custom and practice test — it is what turns a discretionary-sounding label into a practice so certain and notorious that employees are taken to have contracted on the basis it would continue.

testPool.prompt: A collective agreement between an employer and a union increases the notice period for redundancy. Dan's individual contract makes no reference to collective agreements at all. Does the change automatically apply to Dan?
options: Yes — collective agreements automatically bind every employee at the workplace
No — without an incorporation clause (express or implied) in Dan's own contract, the collective agreement does not bind him individually
Yes, but only if Dan is a member of the union that negotiated it
testPool.explanation: Following Galley, incorporation requires a route from the collective agreement into the individual contract. With no incorporation clause, express or implied through custom and practice, the collective agreement has no automatic effect on Dan's own terms.

testPool.prompt: Fatima's contract states her terms 'shall include those agreed from time to time' between her employer and the recognised union. A new collective agreement reduces overtime rates. Is Fatima bound by the change?
options: No — a variation that is unfavourable to the employee can never be incorporated, however the clause is worded
Yes — following Galley, an express 'from time to time' incorporation clause binds the employee to future collectively agreed variations without separate individual consent
Only if Fatima personally votes in favour of the new agreement
testPool.explanation: Galley establishes that a 'from time to time' incorporation clause captures future collective variations, not just the terms in force at the point of signing, and that no fresh individual consent is required — the employee's consent was given in advance through the incorporation clause itself.

testPool.prompt: Josh's written contract states he has 'no entitlement to a lunch break'. In practice, every employee at his workplace, including Josh, has taken a paid 30-minute lunch break at the same time each day for the last four years, and management has never objected. Analyse whether Josh has an enforceable right to that break.
factsToOrder: The written contract says there is no entitlement to a lunch break
A 30-minute paid lunch break has been taken consistently for four years
Management has never objected to the practice

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a consistent workplace practice of paid lunch breaks has become an implied term, despite a contrary written clause.
modelAnswer.rule: Under Autoclenz, a written term can be displaced by evidence, including subsequent conduct, showing it does not reflect the true agreement; separately, a practice that is reasonable, certain and notorious can become an implied term by custom and practice.
modelAnswer.application: Four years of consistent, unchallenged, paid lunch breaks — known to and accepted by management — is reasonable, certain and well established. Combined with Autoclenz's reality-over-wording approach, this practice is strong evidence that the written 'no entitlement' clause does not reflect what was actually agreed and practised.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Josh is likely to have an enforceable implied term to the paid lunch break, notwithstanding the contrary wording in the written contract.

testPool.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a term implied by law from a term implied in fact?
options: A term implied by law applies to employment contracts as a class, regardless of these particular parties' intentions; a term implied in fact fills a gap based on necessity or established practice specific to this contract
A term implied by law can be excluded by any express clause saying so, in every case
There is no meaningful distinction — both are simply 'implied terms'
testPool.trapExplanation: Collapsing the two categories is the most common error here. Terms implied by law (like mutual trust and confidence) attach because the contract is an employment contract; terms implied in fact are specific to the facts of this particular agreement, whether through necessity (business efficacy) or established custom and practice.

testPool.prompt: In the extract from National Coal Board v Galley below, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
testPool.passage: Where the individual contract of employment expressly provides that terms shall be those agreed between the employer and the union from time to time, the employee is bound by a subsequent collective variation without any requirement of fresh, individual consent to that specific change, because consent to the process of collective variation was given in advance through the incorporation clause itself.
testPool.ratioSentence: Where the individual contract of employment expressly provides that terms shall be those agreed between the employer and the union from time to time, the employee is bound by a subsequent collective variation without any requirement of fresh, individual consent to that specific change.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating the written contract, or the s 1 statement, as automatically decisive. Both are strong starting evidence, not the end of the enquiry — check whether custom, practice, or an incorporation clause has quietly changed what's actually binding.
